title: Seller Financing Addendum
summary: Add owner financing terms to a purchase contract: down payment, rate, amortization, balloon, security, insurance and compliance.
useWhen: The seller will carry back a note for part of the purchase price, secured by a mortgage or deed of trust on the property.
watchOuts: Federal law: seller financing of a consumer's home can make the seller a 'loan originator' and a creditor subject to ability-to-repay rules. Regulation Z excludes a natural person, estate or trust financing one property in 12 months (no negative amortization, fixed rate or limited adjustable rate), and a person financing up to three properties (fully amortizing, good-faith ability-to-repay determination, so no balloon). Outside those exclusions, use a licensed mortgage loan originator.
State law: many states have their own SAFE Act licensing and lending rules for seller financing (for example Texas Finance Code ch. 156/157/180 and ch. 159 for wraps). Verify locally.
If the seller still has a mortgage on the property, this is really a wraparound. Use the wraparound addendum, because the existing lender's due-on-sale clause applies.
The security instrument (mortgage or deed of trust) is state-specific, must be drafted for the property's state, signed with notarization and recorded. This addendum does not create a lien by itself.
Balloon payments are a common cause of buyer default. Make sure the buyer has a realistic plan to refinance.
Use a third-party loan servicer for payment records, escrow, Form 1098 reporting and year-end statements.

variables.label: State where the property is located
variables.help: Two-letter code. Massless shows the notes for this state from the state reference (states.json): official forms, required disclosures, closing practice, notarization and recording, executory-contract and wholesaling rules.

variables.label: Down payment
variables.help: Cash at closing, including earnest money.

variables.label: Rate type
variables.help: The Reg Z exclusions require a fixed rate or one that adjusts only after 5+ years with reasonable caps.

variables.label: Amortization (years)
variables.help: Schedule used to calculate the payment.

variables.label: Balloon payment?
variables.help: Entire balance due before the loan fully amortizes. Not allowed under the three-property exclusion.

variables.label: Buyer pays monthly escrow for taxes and insurance?
Late fee
variables.default: 5% of the payment if more than 15 days late

variables.label: Lien position
options: second lien behind a new buyer loan

variables.label: Security instrument
options: the instrument customary in the state of the property

variables.label: Federal lending-law path
options: loan originated by a licensed mortgage loan originator
variables.help: Reg Z 12 CFR 1026.36(a)(4)-(5) excludes some seller financers from loan-originator rules if conditions are met. State SAFE Act and licensing laws may still apply. Verify with an attorney.

variables.label: Buyer provides credit report, income and asset documentation?
Include a due-on-sale clause in the seller's note?
variables.help: Seller can call the note due if buyer transfers the property.

sections.title: 1. Addendum
sections.body: This addendum, dated {{addendum_date}}, is part of the purchase contract dated {{contract_date}} between {{buyer_name}} ("Buyer") and {{seller_name}} ("Seller") for {{property_address}}, {{state}}. If it conflicts with the purchase contract, this addendum controls.

sections.title: 2. Financing terms
3. Balloon payment
sections.body: **The entire unpaid balance is due {{balloon_months}} months after the first payment date.** Buyer understands that the regular payments will not pay off the loan by then, and that Buyer will need to refinance, sell or otherwise pay the balance. Seller has no obligation to extend or refinance. Buyer: [[initial:buyer]]

sections.title: 4. Note and security
sections.body: At closing Buyer will sign a promissory note for the amount financed, and a {{security_instrument}} securing it as a {{lien_position}} on the Property. Both will be prepared by an attorney or title professional licensed in {{state}}, in the form customary there. The security instrument will be notarized and recorded in the county records at closing. Seller may obtain a lender's title insurance policy at Seller's expense, unless the purchase contract says otherwise.

sections.title: 5. Due-on-sale in Seller's note
sections.body: The note and security instrument will allow Seller to require payment in full if Buyer sells or transfers the Property or an interest in it without Seller's written consent, except transfers that federal law protects.

sections.title: 6. Escrow for taxes and insurance
sections.body: Buyer will pay one-twelfth of the estimated annual property taxes and insurance premiums with each monthly payment, into an escrow account held by the servicer, which will pay those bills when due and provide an annual escrow statement.

sections.title: 7. Insurance and maintenance
sections.body: Buyer will keep the Property insured for full replacement cost, with Seller named as mortgagee or loss payee, keep it in good repair, pay taxes and assessments before they are delinquent, and not commit waste. If Buyer fails to, Seller may pay and add the cost to the loan balance.

sections.title: 8. Buyer's credit and ability to repay
sections.body: Within 5 days after the Effective Date of the purchase contract, Buyer will give Seller a current credit report, proof of income (pay stubs, tax returns or bank statements), and a list of debts. Seller will make a good-faith determination that Buyer can reasonably repay the loan. Seller may terminate the purchase contract within 5 days after receiving the documents if Seller reasonably determines Buyer cannot repay, and Buyer receives the earnest money back. Buyer authorizes Seller to obtain Buyer's credit report for this purpose. Buyer: [[initial:buyer]]

sections.title: 9. Lending-law compliance
sections.body: The parties intend this loan to comply with federal and state lending law using this path: **{{compliance_path}}**. Each party has had the opportunity to consult an attorney about Regulation Z (including 12 CFR 1026.36(a)(4)-(5) and 1026.43), the SAFE Act and the licensing and disclosure laws of {{state}}. If a licensed mortgage loan originator is required, Seller will engage one and the loan terms will be adjusted as needed to comply. Seller: [[initial:seller]] Buyer: [[initial:buyer]]

sections.title: 10. Servicing
sections.body: Payments will be made to {{servicer}} (if named), which will keep payment records, provide year-end interest statements, and handle escrow. Servicing fees are paid as the parties agree in writing.

sections.title: 11. Existing liens
sections.body: Seller confirms there is no existing mortgage or lien on the Property that will remain after closing. If there is, the parties will instead use a wraparound addendum, because the existing lender's rights are affected. Seller: [[initial:seller]]

sections.title: 12. Default
sections.body: Default, notice, cure and foreclosure will follow the note, the security instrument and the law of {{state}}. Seller will give Buyer at least 30 days' written notice and opportunity to cure a payment default before accelerating, or longer if the law requires.

sections.title: 13. State-specific requirements
sections.body: The property is in {{state}}. The parties will comply with that state's requirements for this transaction, including required seller disclosures and forms, licensing rules, closing and recording requirements, and any mandatory statutory notices. Massless shows a summary of known requirements for {{state}} with this template. That summary is a starting point, may be incomplete or out of date, and is not part of this agreement. Any addendum or disclosure form the state requires will be attached and signed by the parties.

sections.title: Signatures
sections.body:
By signing below, each party agrees to this document.

**Buyer** — {{buyer_name}}

[[sig:buyer]]

Printed name: [[name:buyer]]
Date: [[date:buyer]]

**Seller** — {{seller_name}}

[[sig:seller]]

Printed name: [[name:seller]]
Date: [[date:seller]]

disclaimer: This is a starting template from the Massless open contract library. It is not legal advice, and using it does not create an attorney-client relationship. Laws vary by state and change over time. Have a licensed attorney in your state review it before you sign. Real estate contracts carry state-specific disclosure, licensing, closing and recording rules. If a real estate licensee is involved, the licensee may be required to use state-promulgated or approved forms instead of this one (for example in Texas and Colorado). Deeds, mortgages and deeds of trust usually must be notarized and recorded; an electronic signature on this document does not record anything. Creative-finance transactions (subject-to, seller financing, wraps, lease-options, contracts for deed) can trigger lender due-on-sale rights, federal and state lending and licensing laws (Truth in Lending/Dodd-Frank, SAFE Act), state executory-contract statutes and consumer-protection claims. Each party, and especially the seller, should have independent legal counsel and a tax adviser before signing.

sources.title: Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.36 (loan originator rules, seller-financer exclusions) (eCFR)
SAFE Act state licensing rules, 12 CFR Part 1008 (eCFR)
Lone Star Land Law: Wraparound regulation in Texas
Garn-St Germain Act due-on-sale provisions, 12 U.S.C. §1701j-3 (Cornell LII)
